item.description:

Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud
October 26, 20262:41 PM ET
Juliana Kim
A SNAP recipient checks her balance left after purchasing food supplies with a California EBT card in Los Angeles on Oct. 31, 2025.
Damian Dovarganes/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Damian Dovarganes/AP
In a major step to combat a form of fraud that has robbed food stamp recipients of millions of dollars, the Trump administration is proposing a requirement for states to bolster the security features on their food assistance cards.
In recent years, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, has been the repeated target of card skimming, when thieves extract personal information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts. Most SNAP cards rely on a magnetic stripe for swipe payment – which tends to be vulnerable to skimming because it does a poor job of securing the data stored on cards.

item.title: Judge says DOJ illegally fired the daughter of former FBI director Comey
item.description:
Law
Judge says DOJ illegally fired the daughter of former FBI director Comey
October 26, 20262:38 PM ET
By
Nate Perez
,
Ryan Lucas
Maurene Comey (R), daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, departs a courthouse in October 2025 in Alexandria, Va.
Win McNamee/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Win McNamee/Getty Images
A New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Justice Department unlawfully fired former prosecutor Maurene Comey, who is the daughter of ex-FBI Director James Comey.
Maurene Comey served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan for around a decade, working on high-profile cases against defendants like Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. The Trump Justice Department fired her in July 2025 despite her consistently receiving accolades from the department for her work.
In response, she sued the Justice Department and others, arguing that her dismissal was unlawful and unconstitutional. Her lawsuit said she was fired because her father is the former FBI director, a prominent critic of President Trump.

item.title: Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
item.description:

Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
October 26, 20269:25 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
FILE - A piece of toast is prepared with Vegemite in Sydney, Australia, Monday, Nov. 17, 2025.
Rick Rycroft/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Rick Rycroft/AP
MELBOURNE, Australia — A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state's ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian."
Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.
He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to "enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background," court documents showed.

Xie Huanchi/Xinhua via AP

HONG KONG — China's political leaders and elites began a four-day meeting Monday to discuss strengthening the ruling Communist Party's discipline, as Chinese President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty and reliability from officials while deepening his yearslong campaign against corruption.
This week's closed-door gathering, known as the fifth plenum of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader and personnel changes to key leadership bodies.
Xi began the meeting by delivering a work report and speaking about a draft policy decision on advancing "full and rigorous party self-governance," according to China's official Xinhua News Agency. The policy aims to make cadres more disciplined, effective and less corrupt.

Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions — and they say the technology is rapidly transforming the field.
When the first hurricane of the Atlantic season formed this month, an AI model beat out traditional models at predicting where it would go.

In early October, Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm. Conventional forecasting models initially predicted it would head further west, toward southeastern Louisiana.

item.title: Loggers say Roadless Rule repeal won't solve their biggest challenges
item.description:
National
Loggers say Roadless Rule repeal won't solve their biggest challenges
October 26, 20265:00 AM ET
Kirk Siegler
Logs from a salvage timber sale after a recent wildfire in the Willamette National Forest in Oregon.
Kirk Siegler
hide caption
toggle caption i
Kirk Siegler
EUGENE, Ore. - President Trump is widely expected to soon open up some 44 million acres of the country's last pristine national forests in a move he says will bring timber jobs back to struggling small towns and help prevent wildfires in overgrown lands.
Trump signaled the move with executive actions last year aimed at dramatically boosting timber sales on U.S. Forest Service land and reversing the agency's 25-year-old Roadless Rule, which blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forestlands.
Today with the formal repeal of the Roadless Rule rule expected early next year, the picture on the ground in timber country looks messier. Those who make a living in the forests say the problems are much bigger than access to more trees.
"I'm not saying these EOs [Executive Orders] are useless, they set the tone," says Sean Smith, CEO of the family owned Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Ore.
